title: Sentence Structure
intro: Build complete sentences and join their ideas correctly.

sections.heading: Clauses and phrases
body: A clause has a subject (who or what it is about) and a verb (an action or state, such as runs or is). An independent clause is a complete thought that can stand alone. A dependent clause needs another clause to finish its thought; it often starts with because, although, if, when, or while.

A phrase is a group of words without a complete subject and verb. Find those two parts first. If removing a starter such as because leaves a complete thought, you had a dependent clause. Do not decide only by where you pause.

examples.text: The excited child opened his present.
examples.label: Independent clause — you can stop here

examples.text: When the excited child opened his present…
examples.label: Dependent clause — the opening word forces you to keep going
Phrase — no subject doing the action

sections.tip: Read it aloud. If you can stop talking, it is an independent clause. If you feel forced to keep going, it is dependent or a phrase.

sections.heading: Sentence fragments
body: Read the entire sentence. It needs a subject, a main verb, and a complete thought; a fragment is missing one of these.
“The student running to class” has no main verb. Add one: “The student running to class dropped her bottle.” An -ed form can be either a past-tense verb or a modifier, so check its job.

examples.text: My little brother Shaun is excited to go to the beach and surf.
examples.label: Complete — has a subject and a working verb

examples.text: Excited to go to the beach and surf.
examples.label: Fragment — no subject

sections.tip: An -ing form needs a helping verb to serve as the main verb. An -ed form may be a past-tense verb or a modifier; check its job in the complete sentence.

sections.heading: Five common clause patterns
body: Two independent clauses: use a period, a semicolon, or comma + FANBOYS (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).

An opening dependent clause usually takes a comma before the main clause. A dependent clause that follows and is needed for the meaning usually takes none. These are five common patterns, not the only possibilities.
A colon or dash can introduce a second clause that explains or emphasizes the first: “She had one concern: the bridge was closed.” Semicolons also separate complex list items.

examples.text: Mary loves dogs. Andrew loves cats.
examples.label: Rule 1 — period between two independents

examples.text: Mary loves dogs; Andrew loves cats.
examples.label: Rule 2 — semicolon between two independents

examples.text: Mary loves dogs, and Andrew loves cats.
examples.label: Rule 3 — comma + FANBOYS

examples.text: While Mary loves dogs, Andrew loves cats.
examples.label: Rule 4 — dependent, comma, independent

examples.text: Mary loves dogs while Andrew loves cats.
examples.label: Rule 5 — independent straight into dependent, no comma

sections.tip: FANBOYS = For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. A FANBOYS word joins two independent clauses only with a comma in front of it.

sections.heading: Comma splices
body: A comma alone between two complete thoughts creates a comma splice. Use a period, semicolon, or comma plus a connecting word such as and or but. You can also make one thought dependent by adding because or although.
However, therefore, and thus connect ideas but are not FANBOYS conjunctions. Between complete thoughts, put a period or semicolon before them. Within one clause, however can sit between commas.

examples.text: Redwoods are among the tallest trees in the world; some have grown 350 feet tall.
examples.label: Fixed with a semicolon

examples.text: Redwoods are among the tallest trees in the world, some have grown 350 feet tall.
examples.label: Comma splice

sections.tip: However, therefore, moreover, and thus are not FANBOYS. When one of these words links two independent clauses, treat it like the start of a new sentence — it needs a semicolon or a period in front of it. (Tucked inside a single clause between commas, however is fine.)

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: When choices change punctuation or add words such as because or which, label each side: independent clause, dependent clause, or phrase.

Check the connection and meaning. Two independent clauses cannot use a comma alone. Colons and dashes can introduce explanations; semicolons joining clauses need complete clauses on both sides. Confirm the structure before relying on your ear.
sections.tip: A semicolon and a period do the same job, so if two choices differ only in that way, eliminate both — the test cannot have two right answers.

check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
check.stem: Penguins are clumsy on land[[,]] they are amazingly graceful in water.
check.explanation: Two independent clauses meet at the underlined spot, and only ', but' supplies the required comma + FANBOYS. NO CHANGE is a comma splice; ', however' is still a comma splice because however is not a FANBOYS word; and '; while' places a semicolon before a dependent clause, but a semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides.

check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
check.stem: While the Egyptian pyramids were built over 4,000 years ago[[, still standing]] today.
check.explanation: The sentence opens with the dependent clause 'While the Egyptian pyramids were built over 4,000 years ago,' so a comma plus an independent clause must follow — ', they still stand' supplies the subject and working verb. NO CHANGE leaves a fragment with no subject; ' they still standing' has no working verb; and '; they still stand' puts a semicolon after a dependent clause, which a semicolon cannot do.

check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
check.stem: Swimming is a great workout[[; it]] works all the major muscle groups.
check.explanation: Both halves are independent clauses, so the semicolon in NO CHANGE correctly joins them. ', it' creates a comma splice; ' it' fuses the clauses with no punctuation at all; and ', however it' is still a comma splice because however is not a FANBOYS word.
